meta.title: The two hours a week nobody has measured
meta.subtitle: A route-planning pitch surfaces a real cost that its own source calls a guess.
extra: ~30 drivers, by the ops manager's own count

abstract:
Ines Vartanian, selling a route-planning service, maps how Hollis Grady's depot runs: a dispatcher hand-builds routes each morning for thirty-something drivers covering high-fifties to sixty stops apiece. The number that matters has no measured basis. Hollis puts driver time lost to re-routing at 'somewhere north of two hours a week,' concentrated on the one account watching the clock.

Nine drivers left last year, a figure he revises downward mid-sentence, and he will not attach a dollar value to it, leaving that to payroll. Ines converts the guess into roughly three thousand hours a year. She proposes a thirty-day pilot on that one route, sent to Hollis directly, before anyone above him approves spending.

verdict.position: The call ended on a thirty-day pilot limited to the northern run, with the economics resting on an estimate Hollis calls a guess and no approver named.
for: 00:45:10 — Hollis says one run, one month with real drivers is something he could take upstairs.
00:42:40 — He names two checkable proof conditions: a week the northern run does not blow up, and the dispatcher off the phone by nine.
00:16:20 — The lost time concentrates on the northern run, which has the tightest addresses and the least room to improvise.
00:14:00 — The northern run is the biggest single account, and two missed windows in a month get raised by someone above Hollis.
against: 00:10:20 — The two-hours-a-week figure is Hollis's guess, and he says it could be less or a lot more.
00:35:00 — The three-thousand-hour annual figure is Ines multiplying two of his loose estimates, not a measured baseline.
00:33:20 — He declines to convert hours into dollars, leaving the business case without a money value.
00:40:00 — He will not name who approves a purchase until the numbers hold up.
verdict.decides_it: The pilot Ines scopes at 00:46:20 would settle it, if it measures re-routing time rather than only the two conditions Hollis named.

insights.title: A guess used as a baseline
insights.claim: The pitch's economics rest on a single unmeasured estimate, which gets multiplied into an annual figure rather than checked.

supports.observation: Hollis offers two-plus hours a week as a guess and says it swings week to week.
Ines multiplies that guess by thirty-two drivers and fifty-two weeks into three thousand hours.
Hollis answers that it sounds worse said out loud than it feels day to day.

insights.implication: Any proposal priced off this figure inherits its uncertainty, so the first job of a pilot is measuring the baseline rather than proving an improvement against it.
insights.basis: The speaker labels his own number a guess at 00:10:20, and no measured source appears in the call.

insights.title: Concentrated, not average, pain
insights.claim: The lost time is concentrated on one account rather than spread across the fleet, which is why a single-route pilot can answer the question.

supports.observation: Hollis says the weekly hours are not what keeps him up; the northern run is.
He confirms the time concentrates there, with the tightest addresses and least room to improvise.
Ines proposes a month on the northern run alone as enough to answer both conditions.

insights.implication: A fleet-wide average would have priced the wrong problem; the buying decision turns on one route's reliability, so that is where the evidence has to come from.
insights.basis: Asserted by the prospect at 00:12:00 and confirmed at 00:16:20, with no routing data behind it.

insights.title: The limits of what he will claim
insights.claim: Hollis hedges or revises every figure he gives, and refuses to convert any of them into money.

supports.observation: Headcount arrives as thirty-something drivers, maybe thirty-two on a normal week.
Turnover is stated as twelve and corrected to nine mid-sentence.
He declines a per-hour rate twice, saying payroll owns that math.

insights.implication: He is reliable about what he does not know, so a proposal that depends on a firm dollar figure needs a different source inside the account.
insights.basis: Three separate hedges and one explicit refusal, all in his own words.

insights.title: A pilot without a named buyer
insights.claim: No approver is named, and the pilot is scoped before anyone establishes who could fund it.

supports.observation: Ines asks whether sign-off is his or goes above him.
Hollis defers, wanting to see the numbers hold up before naming an approver.
He asks for the scope by direct message, since the group inbox would sit for two weeks.

insights.implication: Work is being committed against an unidentified buyer, so the pilot's result has to be something Hollis can carry upward on his own.
insights.basis: The deferral is explicit at 00:40:00 and no name appears anywhere later in the call.

acts.title: Mapping the manual morning
acts.summary: Ines maps the depot's manual process: a dispatcher hand-builds routes for thirty-something drivers. Hollis offers the ongoing repair cost as a guess — north of two hours a week — rather than a measured figure.

turning_point.text: Somewhere north of two hours a week, I'd guess, fixing a route that fell apart

acts.title: Where it concentrates, and what it costs
acts.summary: The loose weekly number turns out to concentrate on one high-value account. Nine drivers left last year, and Ines converts the guess into an annual hours figure while Hollis refuses to price it in dollars.

turning_point.text: that's north of three thousand hours a year sitting in re-routing

acts.title: Deflection, proof conditions, and a narrow pilot
acts.summary: Hollis defers naming a purchase approver until the numbers hold up, then sets two checkable conditions for belief. They agree to scope a thirty-day pilot on the northern run alone.

threads.name: The loose weekly number
threads.what: Hollis estimates driver time lost to re-routing at 'somewhere north of two hours a week' and never offers a firmer figure.
threads.why_it_matters: The whole pitch's economics end up resting on a number its own source calls a guess.

threads.name: Who signs off
threads.what: Ines asks who approves a purchase like this and Hollis defers naming anyone until results are proven.
threads.why_it_matters: A pilot scoped before a real approver is named risks being work with no buyer at the end of it.

threads.name: Turnover as a second cost
threads.what: Nine drivers left the depot last year, a figure Hollis revises down from twelve mid-sentence, and attributes only partly to routing.
threads.why_it_matters: It gives the pitch a cost angle beyond the weekly hours, but one Hollis is careful not to fully claim.

evidence.claim: Re-routing costs each driver roughly two-plus hours a week.
evidence.evidence: Hollis offers it unprompted as his own guess, explicitly not a measured figure.

evidence.claim: The re-routing time is not spread evenly — it concentrates on the northern run.
evidence.evidence: Hollis confirms directly when Ines asks whether the two hours are evenly spread.

evidence.claim: Driver turnover last year was about nine, partly related to routing unpredictability.
evidence.evidence: Hollis states it while revising the number downward mid-sentence, and qualifies the routing link himself.

signals.signal: Hollis draws a hard line at translating hours into dollars, twice pointing to payroll rather than estimating a rate himself.

numbers.means: Hollis's own headcount estimate for a normal week; no roster figure was checked or given.

numbers.value: ~55-60 stops/driver/day (stated as 'high fifties, maybe sixty... give or take')
numbers.means: A per-driver daily stop count offered as a loose range, with the northern run flagged as heavier than the average.

numbers.value: ~2+ hrs/week/driver (stated as 'somewhere north of two hours a week, I'd guess')
numbers.means: Hollis's own estimate of driver time lost to re-routing; explicitly a guess, not a measured baseline, and he says it varies week to week.

numbers.value: 9 drivers/year turnover (revised down mid-sentence from an initial 'twelve')
numbers.means: Last year's driver turnover count, self-corrected on the call; Hollis attributes only some of it to routing, not all.

numbers.value: ~3,000+ hrs/year (Ines's arithmetic: ~30 drivers x ~2 hrs/week x 52 weeks)
numbers.means: A derived annual figure built by multiplying two of Hollis's own loose estimates; not independently confirmed beyond his 'sounds worse than it feels' reaction.

diarization.why: Hollis's reaction to the annual-hours figure and Ines's pivot to the sign-off question land back to back; the topic change reads as Ines moving on before Hollis finished.

next_steps.commitment: Ines will scope a thirty-day pilot limited to the northern run and send it to Hollis directly rather than the group inbox.

aligned_on: The manual process is a dispatcher hand-building routes every morning for thirty-something drivers.
The re-routing time is concentrated on the northern run, the account that matters most to Hollis.
unresolved: Whether the two-hours-a-week figure would hold up to actual measurement.
Who signs off on a purchase like this.

risks.note: She built a roughly three-thousand-hour annual figure by multiplying two of Hollis's own guesses, not a measured baseline.
He has agreed to a pilot before knowing whether anyone above him will approve funding it.
